columns.title: The situation rhymes with things you've seen, but a few details are different this time. You'd more likely:
answers: Check the numbers on the parts that differ, go on experience for the rest.
Treat it as close enough to what you know and decide on that basis.

columns.title: You're starting a piece of work you could do on your own. You're more likely to:
answers: Just get going on it yourself.
Talk it through with someone first.

columns.title: Something you put together recently works, but not well. You're more likely to:
answers: Take another pass at the parts that are weakest.
Start it over with a different idea of how it should work.

columns.title: That tempo turns out to be the normal state of the team -- it's been a couple of months and it hasn't let up. You'd more likely:
answers: Have found you'd rather keep it this way than go back.
Be looking to carve out slower stretches for yourself.

columns.title: Your work is being reviewed in a meeting with the rest of the team present. When they've spotted something you got wrong, you'd rather they:
answers: Note it privately afterwards, rather than in front of the whole group.
Say it there in the room while everyone's looking at the same thing.

columns.title: You're given a project that a few other teams are depending on, and people will notice if it goes wrong. You're more likely to:
answers: Set the direction yourself and keep people posted as you go.
Agree the direction with your manager before you start.

columns.title: Something the team relies on works well and nobody is complaining. You've thought of a fundamentally different approach that might be better, but you'd have to throw the current one out to find out. You'd more likely:
answers: Push to try the new approach.

columns.title: On the teams you've been on, the decisions that frustrated you were the ones where:
answers: A call sat unmade while people waited on figures that were never going to arrive in a usable form.
A call was made on somebody's read of it, with no way for anyone to check the reasoning after.

columns.title: Thinking about the stretches of work that wore you down, what actually did it was:
answers: A tempo that never dropped, month after month, with no stretch you could exhale in.
Long stretches where the work was there but nothing was urgent, and the days ran together.

columns.title: A piece of work could either be split up and done separately, or done start-to-finish with someone else in the room the whole time. Same deadline either way. You'd pick:
answers: Split it up and sync at the end.

columns.title: There's something small you could be doing better. You'd rather your manager:
answers: Mention it next time you're already talking one-on-one.
Send it over as soon as they notice, without waiting for a scheduled slot.

columns.title: You're given a routine task you've handled many times before, with no special instructions attached. You're more likely to:
answers: Just do it your usual way without checking in.

columns.title: A process that's been running for a year does the job, though nobody loves it. You'd more likely:
answers: Replace it with something you think would work better.
Smooth out the parts that annoy people and leave the rest.

columns.title: The team proposes a standing hour every day where everyone works through the current problem together. For you that would be:
answers: Worth the hour -- you'd get more out of it than you'd lose.
An hour you'd rather have back for your own work.

columns.title: The people you've worked under that you've found hardest were the ones who:
answers: Never told you where you stood until something formal came around, so you were guessing for months at a time.
Raised things the moment they saw them, wherever you happened to be and whoever happened to be there.

columns.title: Looking back, what's frustrated you most was when:
answers: You were left to figure out something high-stakes entirely on your own, with no one available even once to sanity-check your read of it before you committed.
Even on the most important work, you were expected to check in and get sign-off on the direction and the plan before starting -- not just the finer details.

columns.title: A single afternoon comes up where several things need turning around quickly at once. Afterwards you'd say:
answers: That's a good afternoon -- you'd take more of them.
That's fine occasionally, but you were glad when it was over.

columns.title: This one is genuinely new -- nobody on the team has faced this exact situation, and there is some data available but it's thin and doesn't cover it cleanly. You'd more likely:
answers: Work from the thin data and say plainly what it does and doesn't cover.
Reason it out from what you know about how situations like this tend to behave.

columns.title: The setups you've worked in that drained you most were the ones where:
answers: Weeks where you barely worked alongside anyone -- your part arrived, you did it, you passed it on.
Almost never getting a stretch of the day that was yours, because the work was always happening in a group.

columns.title: A push like that runs for a full week rather than an afternoon. Partway through, you're more likely to be:
answers: Watching the calendar for when it eases off.
Still running on it without particularly wanting it to stop.

columns.title: You've just handed in a piece of work and there's a real problem with it. You'd rather find out:
answers: Straight away, before you've moved on to anything else.
Once they've been through all of it, in one go.

columns.title: You've been most frustrated in situations where:
answers: Things kept getting rebuilt from scratch, and work you'd already finished got thrown away over and over.
Nothing could be rebuilt, so you kept working around the same known problems because replacing them was never worth it.

columns.title: A call comes up that's close to ones you've made many times before, and it points the way it usually does. You'd more likely:
answers: Go with what the pattern has been, without pulling it up.
Pull the figures first, even though you expect them to agree.

columns.title: You're handed a new project that's fairly low-risk if something goes wrong. You're more likely to:
answers: Check your approach with your manager first.
Figure out your own approach as you go.

columns.title: Where are you in your career?
How big is the organization you work for — the whole organization, not your team?
answers: An early-stage startup — a handful of people, still finding its footing.
A small company that has found its footing and is growing — tens of people.
A mid-sized organization — hundreds of people, with real structure in place.
A large organization — thousands of people, established in its market.
A very large enterprise — tens of thousands of people and many layers.

columns.title: Compared with what you could earn elsewhere doing similar work, how does this role pay?
answers: Well below what you could get elsewhere for similar work.
Well above what you could get elsewhere for similar work.

columns.title: Which industry is the organization you work for in?
answers: Technology — software, hardware, internet or IT services.
Finance — banking, insurance, investment or accounting.
Healthcare — hospitals, clinics, pharma or health services.
Retail — shops, e-commerce or consumer goods.
Not sure, or I’d rather not say.

columns.title: How much say do you have over how your work gets done?
answers: Your work is assigned and specified for you, and most decisions go up for sign-off before you act.
Your manager sets the direction and the priorities; you choose your own tactics inside clear guardrails.
Direction is set at the team level, and within that you pick how the work gets done.
You own the outcome and choose your own approach, with only light approval along the way.
You set your own priorities and your own methods, and almost nothing needs approval.

columns.title: Who decides what you work on, and in what order?
answers: You decide what you take on and in what order; nobody hands you a queue.
You’re given the outcomes to hit, and the sequence and the timing are yours.
You and your manager set your priorities together, and either of you can move them.
Your priorities are set for you, though you can make the case for changing them.
What you work on and when is scheduled for you, and changing it takes permission.

columns.title: What is the tempo of the work?
answers: The tempo is fast: aggressive deadlines, quick turnaround, and an intense week.
Urgency is regular — timelines are tight-ish and work goes out often, without being relentless.
The tempo is ordinary: some stretches of crunch, some stretches of calm.
The tempo is generally measured, with occasional pushes; deadlines exist but rarely dominate the week.
The tempo is deliberate: long planning horizons and an unhurried week.

columns.title: How quickly are things expected to happen?
answers: Nothing is expected in a hurry — requests can wait until you get to them.
Most things can wait a day or two; a genuine rush is the exception.
Some things need an answer the same day, some can sit for a week.
Quick turnaround is the norm — you’re expected to respond and move within the day.
Requests land expecting an answer now, and your week can be rearranged overnight.

columns.title: How does the work actually get produced?
answers: You produce your work heads-down and alone; meetings are rare and there is no pairing or joint working time.
You produce the work alone and bring it to periodic syncs; those meetings are status and handoff, not joint problem-solving.
Roughly half the work is done alone and half of it in a group; neither mode dominates how the work gets made.
Cross-functional work is common and meetings are frequent; most problems get worked through as a group.
Almost everything is produced together — constant pairing, standing group sessions, a team you are working alongside all day.

columns.title: How much of your working day is spent working with other people?
answers: Most of the day is live time with other people — calls, working sessions, back-and-forth throughout.
You’re in live working sessions with others most days, with time in between to work on your own.
It is an even mix of live group time and written, work-on-your-own time.
It is mostly written and asynchronous, with a live session when something needs one.
Written updates stand in for meetings almost entirely, and long stretches of solo time are the norm.

columns.title: How often do you hear how your work is landing?
answers: Rarely — you hear about your work occasionally, and often only when something has gone wrong.
Feedback arrives mainly on a fixed cycle: a review, or a scheduled check-in.
A normal mix: scheduled reviews, plus comment in the moment when something comes up.
Often — you get comment on your work well outside any review cycle.
Constantly — you hear how the work is landing as you go, from whoever is looking at it.

columns.title: How is criticism of your work delivered?
answers: Criticism is delivered straight and unsoftened, and open disagreement about the work is routine.
Criticism is fairly direct and debate about the work is normal; a thick skin helps.
Criticism is delivered plainly and in moderation — neither blunt nor heavily cushioned.
Criticism is delivered diplomatically; directness is the exception.
Criticism is cushioned or indirect when it comes, and open disagreement is rare.

columns.title: What kind of work is it — improving what exists, or making what doesn’t?
answers: Creating things that don’t exist yet — new offerings, new capabilities, bets that may not come off.
Building something new comes up often, alongside the work of running what already exists.
A real split: part of the work improves what exists, part of it creates something new.
Mostly improving what already exists, with the occasional genuinely new thing at the edges.
Making something that already exists work better — improvement and scale, not new territory.

columns.title: How much of the work is a bet that might not pay off?
answers: Almost none — work that doesn’t pan out isn’t planned for, and what gets started is expected to land.
The occasional experiment is tolerated, but the bulk of the effort goes to things with a known payoff.
Some of the work is a known quantity and some of it is a bet; both are normal.
Experiments are a planned part of the work, and some of them are expected not to pan out.
Exploration is the point — a good share of what is tried is expected to fail, and that is budgeted for.

columns.title: What do decisions actually rest on?
answers: Taste, experience and vision — someone’s judgement carries the call.
Judgement leads, and numbers are brought in afterwards to confirm it.
Judgement and evidence both carry weight, depending on the call.
Measurement usually settles it, with judgement filling the gaps the numbers don’t cover.
Numbers settle it — measured, tested, and not decided until the evidence is in.

columns.title: When you want to make a case for something, what carries it?
answers: Numbers — you’re expected to bring measurements, tests or analysis.
Usually evidence, though a well-argued judgement call can carry.
Either a strong argument or good numbers will carry a case; both are ordinary currency.
Mostly reasoning and experience; numbers are supporting material.
Argument and instinct — the numbers are rarely what decides it.

All things considered, how satisfied are you with this job?
How well do you think you’re performing in this role?
How energised are you by the work itself?
